name: Judiciary
description: Iran’s judiciary is constitutionally separate from the presidential administration, with its head appointed by the Supreme Leader. Understanding it requires distinguishing its formal responsibilities from documented shortcomings in independence and access to justice. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Iran’s Judiciary: Structure, Powers and Accountability | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s constitutional judicial structure, its relationship with the government, and documented concerns about judicial independence.

content.heading: A separate branch with an appointed leadership
content.content:
Article 156 describes the judiciary as independent and assigns it dispute resolution, protection of public rights, prosecution, supervision of law enforcement and crime prevention. Under Article 157, the Supreme Leader appoints its head for five years; the appointee must be a qualified Islamic jurist with judicial knowledge and administrative ability. [s1]

The judiciary head organizes the branch, prepares judicial bills and administers judicial appointments. The justice minister instead manages relationships with the executive and legislature, selected from candidates proposed by the judiciary head. Holding a cabinet portfolio therefore does not make the minister head of the courts. [s1]

content.heading: Different forms of judicial oversight
content.content:
The Supreme Court supervises courts’ implementation of law and consistency of procedure. The Court of Administrative Justice addresses complaints concerning government officials, bodies and regulations. The General Inspectorate supervises administrative conduct and implementation of laws. Their detailed powers depend on legislation. [s1]

Constitutional safeguards include reasoned judgments, generally public hearings subject to exceptions, and protection against retroactive criminalization. These provisions establish legal standards; they do not demonstrate compliance in individual proceedings. [s1]

content.heading: Formal safeguards and documented practice
content.content:
The United Nations Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran reached a sharply critical assessment in its March 2025 findings concerning the protests that began in September 2022 and their aftermath. Its published summary described a judiciary fundamentally lacking independence, continued judicial harassment of victims and families, and intimidation of people seeking accountability. [s2]

The mission acknowledged some efforts toward accountability and compensation but assessed domestic avenues for redress as inadequate. It also reported exchanges with a presidentially appointed investigative committee while concluding that reparations remained insufficient. These are attributed investigative findings about a defined body of events, rather than an assessment of every civil or criminal case. [s2]

For readers, the central distinction is between an institution’s constitutional mandate and evidence about its operation. Appointment rules explain where formal authority sits; investigation of actual proceedings is needed to evaluate fair treatment, effective remedies and accountability. The material inspected here supports that distinction but does not provide a comprehensive account through the editorial cutoff. [s1][s2]

name: Presidency
description: Iran’s presidency combines an electoral mandate with responsibility for executive administration, within a constitutional system that reserves substantial authority to the Supreme Leader. Its practical influence also depends on cooperation with parliament and other centers of power. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Iran’s Presidency: Election, Responsibilities and Limits | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the constitutional role of Iran’s president, the boundaries of executive authority, and the negotiations involved in governing.

content.heading: An elected office within a wider hierarchy
content.content: Article 113 places the president below the Leadership and assigns executive authority except in matters directly belonging to that office. Presidents are directly elected for four years and may serve only one immediately consecutive additional term. Election requires an absolute majority, with a runoff if necessary. The Guardian Council supervises presidential elections, while Article 110 assigns it confirmation of candidates’ constitutional qualifications. [s1]

content.heading: Administrative responsibility and its boundaries
content.content:
The president heads the Council of Ministers and is responsible for national planning, budgeting and state employment affairs. The constitution also assigns duties involving legislation, diplomatic appointments and international agreements, subject to specified procedures and parliamentary approval where required. [s1]

Presiding over the Supreme National Security Council does not confer unrestricted security authority: its policies operate within the Leader’s general policies, and its decisions require the Leader’s confirmation. [s1]

For presidential incapacity or vacancy covered by Article 131, the first vice-president assumes presidential functions with the Leader’s approval. A council comprising that official, the parliamentary speaker and judiciary head must arrange an election within fifty days. [s1]

content.heading: Why election and governing capacity differ
content.content:
Government formation in 2024 illustrates the political negotiation surrounding the office. Associated Press reporting described parliament’s approval of Masoud Pezeshkian’s cabinet as an early success achieved through choices acceptable to different centers of power. The report also described disagreement within his own political camp over those choices. Its interpretation was that the resulting team emphasized consensus. [s2]

This example helps explain why a presidential election result cannot by itself establish how much of a political program will become policy. Choosing a minister, securing legislative support and implementing a decision are different stages. A report of agreement at one stage does not prove durable cooperation or a completed policy outcome. [s1][s2]

The office is therefore best understood by asking two questions together: what responsibilities does the constitutional text allocate, and what evidence shows how a particular administration exercised them? This page establishes the principal formal responsibilities and offers a dated example of political bargaining. It does not verify the incumbent’s full record or the distribution of practical influence at the editorial cutoff. [s1][s2]

name: Cabinet
description: Iran’s cabinet, constitutionally described as the Council of Ministers, coordinates executive policy under the president. Ministers require parliamentary confidence, and their administrative regulations must remain within the law. [s1]

seo.title: Iran’s Cabinet: Ministers, Confidence Votes and Decisions | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Learn how Iran’s Council of Ministers is formed, how ministers answer to parliament, and how cabinet decisions differ from legislation.

content.heading: How a minister takes office
content.content:
Under Article 133, the president appoints ministers and presents them to parliament for confidence votes. Law determines ministerial numbers and responsibilities; election of a new parliament does not itself require renewed confidence. The president heads the Council of Ministers and coordinates government policy. [s1]

Ministers answer to both the president and parliament. The president may dismiss them, but replacements require parliamentary confidence. Changing half the cabinet after its confidence vote triggers a fresh government confidence vote. A ministry without a minister may have a presidentially appointed caretaker for up to three months. [s1]

content.heading: Collective decisions within legal limits
content.content:
Article 138 authorizes administrative and implementing regulations, which must conform to law. Cabinet regulations and specified ministerial commission decisions are communicated to the parliamentary speaker for review of consistency with legislation. Ministers also bear responsibility for decisions approved collectively. [s1]

This distinguishes cabinet administration from legislation: a government regulation cannot legitimately substitute for a legal amendment. Confidence votes concern political accountability, while review of regulations concerns legal limits. These mechanisms address different questions and do not by themselves establish effective oversight. [s1]

content.heading: A documented formation episode
content.content:
On 21 August 2024, parliament approved all nineteen ministers proposed by President Masoud Pezeshkian, according to Iran Press’s contemporaneous report. Its list covered portfolios ranging from education and health to petroleum, intelligence, foreign affairs and roads and urban development. The breadth of that list illustrates the cabinet’s administrative reach, but does not establish that every state institution falls under ministerial command. [s2]

Independent reporting by Associated Press described the appointments as a negotiated consensus and identified continuity with the preceding administration in several portfolios. Those observations concern the composition and politics of the initial team. They are not evidence that the same individuals remained in office at the editorial cutoff. [s3]

When reading a cabinet announcement, distinguish nomination, parliamentary approval and subsequent tenure. Likewise, an approved ministerial program is an undertaking whose implementation needs separate evidence. The initial confidence vote is a documented institutional event; judging service delivery or policy effectiveness requires budgets, implementation records and outcomes. [s1][s2][s3]
